newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai holds China Coast cricket tournament.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai holds China Coast cricket tournament.

text.p: The revived Shanghai Cricket Club held the first China Coast tournament over the weekend featuring eight six-a-side teams in a match organisers hope will one day encourage China to take up the sport.

The teams, including two from Hong Kong and one each from Wuhan and Beijing, sweated their way through the two-day tournament under the blazing sun on a suburban soccer pitch renamed the Meilong Cricket Ground for the occasion.

"It's the first six's competition in Shanghai ever, and the first time we have gathered together teams from Hong Kong and other cities of mainland China together to play cricket," said Richard Graham, captain of the resurrected Shanghai Cricket Club.
"The Beijing team is skippered by a 100 percent Chinese named Bruce Wong, who spent a few years in Australia where he picked up his English name and the rules of cricket," Graham added.
The historical echoes of the Shanghai Cricket Club are poignant.

In the Shanghai of old, before the communists arrived in 1949, the east China port city had three cricket teams, and a prosperous Shanghai Cricket Club that was one of the centres of social life for the large foreign community of the day.
Instead of an inaccessible soccer ground, games in those days were played in the middle of the racecourse in central Shanghai.
The first cricket tournament in Shanghai since the communist takeover was in 1994, and there have been occasional games since then against Hong Kong and Being in the intervening years.
Graham said he hoped the tournament would help to spark interest in the sport amongst Chinese people.
"Cricket will become an Olympic sport before too long and when it is, the Chinese will be interested in it," he said.

A couple of local Shanghainese onlookers were perplexed by the rules and pointed out that even baseball has failed to make any serious inroads into the mainland Chinese sporting scene, despite its huge success in Taiwan.
